answer: A pre-fix defect could fail lock acquisition under Windows contention because EPERM was not retried: openSync(lockPath,'wx') returns EPERM rather than EEXIST while another process holds or releases the lock, and the retry loop was keyed only on EEXIST. The instrumented matrix reproduced that defect on run 19 of a declared 40 — one child of six, 507ms, no duplicate ID, the other five allocating distinct IDs — so serialisation remained intact IN THE REPRODUCED EVENT. ⚠️ The ORIGINAL 2026-08-18 occurrence remains UNCLASSIFIABLE: its output was never captured, so nothing observed distinguishes this defect from any other cause. What can be said is that this defect explains its observed shape — a full-suite run failing with no duplicate ID reported — and that it did not recur across the bounded post-fix matrix of 80 runs. Fix: retry EEXIST/EPERM/EBUSY/EACCES on acquisition, the same family as #72's rename retry. The maxWaitMs 10s->30s mitigation addressed a timeout not present in the reproduced failure and is reverted.
notes: Reopening condition: any recurrence after the fix. Bounded non-reproduction only — 80 post-fix runs across three cells, which at a 10% per-run rate would miss a recurrence about 4% of the time. ⚠️ EVD-0003, the original failure, supports 'the test failed once' and NOTHING about why. It refutes AST-0003 and is deliberately not linked to AST-0004: an unclassifiable observation cannot bear on a claim about a cause (#101). Answering this question did not make that record classifiable in hindsight.
statement: What caused the single observed failure of the separate-process concurrency test during a full parallel run on 2026-08-18, and is serialisation implicated at all?
title: Why did the concurrency test fail once under full-suite parallel load?

answer: YES, in `next dev`, with one condition the framework does not supply. Measured across a 2x2 matrix (fs.readFileSync / await readFile x cacheComponents disabled / enabled) on Next.js 16.3.1, React 19.2.8, Node v24.18.0, Windows 11: all four cells re-read the file and returned the new value on a fresh request, with server-side counters confirming a genuine re-read rather than a replay. No stale server state, no reliance on HMR, and no framework caching interfered — including with Cache Components enabled and a synchronous read, which the documentation says would be prerendered. THE CONDITION: an external write alone produces nothing — no request, no re-render, no browser update in a 10-second window, in every cell. The application must supply the change signal itself. An SSE route watching the data directory delivered the event to a connected client in both modes, and a reload then showed the new value. That is precisely what the framework-free skeleton already does, so the pattern carries over rather than needing replacement. ⚠️ SCOPED TO `next dev`. AST-0010 carries the production-build claim and is untested; the documentation describes build-time prerendering, and whether this product ever runs a production build is itself undecided given #2 and #22's local-only stance.
notes: Reopening condition: adopting `next build` for any part of the app, or upgrading Next.js past 16.3.1. ⚠️ WRITE-BACK HALF ADDED 2026-08-18 after review pointed out the first answer proved only the read/refresh side. AST-0012 now carries it, measured in both cacheComponents modes: reviewStatus-only boundary held, non-reviewStatus values refused, lock released, no temp file, and the Next.js write BLOCKED while an external process held the lock and completed after release. #100's specific worry — React's state model against #78's lock — did not materialise.
statement: Can a Next.js development app reliably reflect artifact files written by an EXTERNAL process, and perform lock-protected status write-backs, without relying on HMR, stale server state, or framework-owned caching?
title: Can a Next.js dev app reflect externally written files and do lock-protected write-backs?

answer: Tier 1 first, behind a typed validation controller owning provision -> execute -> observe -> destroy, refusing jobs above the approved ceiling before provisioning. Jobs are declared (tier, inputs, argument-array commands, capture plan, limits, expected outputs, network/credential/cost needs); the specialist never gets a shell. Tier 1 is a temp workspace plus a Python venv, which isolates dependencies and is NOT an OS security sandbox — so it makes no containment, filesystem or network-isolation claim, and claims needing those require a higher tier. Every run yields an observation record whose capture plan makes omissions detectable: not captured / not observable / unavailable / redacted, each with a reason. Cleanup failure is a first-class result: keep the evidence, report the retained path. See DEC-0005.
notes: BLOCKING under DEC-0002. BOUNDARIES BEFORE MECHANISM (DEC-0003): (a) what may execute; (b) filesystem/network/credential boundaries per tier (#56) and what a tier may NOT reach; (c) resource limits — time, cost, instance count — since #77's authorisation is meaningless without them; (d) cleanup via #56's `destroy`, and what happens when it fails; (e) ⚠️ AN EVIDENCE-SURVIVAL CONTRACT (#122). What survives a run: environment facts, tool and runtime VERSIONS, inputs, outputs, exit status, timing, permission denials, and explicit omission or redaction reasons. ⚠️ Stated precisely: an absent fact does NOT make the record inapplicable. It stays applicable with an `unknown` comparison; what the absence changes is the attainable RUNG, capping it below environment-matched. So a silent omission decides how strong a claim can ever become, invisibly. ⚠️ And the recorded states describe the OBSERVER, never relevance. Relevance is claim-relative (#105) — the same record may be decisive for another assertion — so `not relevant` is not something evidence can hold. The honest states are: not captured · not observable · unavailable · redacted, with a reason. The applicability layer decides whether the gap matters to a given claim. ⚠️ Which of those states to declare is part of THIS question, because only the states a sandbox can genuinely DETECT are worth declaring — declaring one nothing can distinguish repeats #121's error of promising a capability the host cannot check. Only after all of this does 'which tier first, implemented how' become answerable. ⚠️ AND THE FIELD'S SHAPE IS GOVERNED BY #123: evidence stores observations and provenance, never what they mean for a claim. So whatever this question settles must record why the OBSERVER lacks a fact, and must not smuggle in polarity, relevance, applicability, verdict or confidence — all of which are derived per claim and would be wrong the moment a second assertion cited the same record.
statement: REQ-0005 requires claims to be testable by execution in a real environment. #56 decides three tiers and #77 decides how they activate, but no controller exists for any of them. Which tier is built first, and what provisions, executes, observes and destroys?
title: What implements sandboxed execution, and which tier first?

answer: Production mode. The shipped configuration is `next build` followed by `next start`; `next dev` is a contributor workflow only. Decided by the PM rather than by further research: AST-0015's artifact mismatch settles it on principle — a shipped configuration should be validated in the mode users receive — and no amount of discovery about long-running development servers could change that. See DEC-0018 for the alternatives and their costs, including the accepted one: AST-0010 becomes owed immediately.
notes: ⚠️ This question is a TRIGGER, not only a choice. AST-0010's deferral is conditioned on the deployment mode staying undeclared; declaring `next build` / `next start` is exactly the reopening condition it records, and the validation becomes owed the moment the answer is production. Answering `next dev` only is therefore cheaper AND narrower, and the cost of that narrowness — no evidence that the shipped configuration is the validated one — belongs in the answer rather than being discovered later. ⚠️ PARTIAL RESULT 2026-08-24 — DIRECT RETRIEVAL ONLY, AND THE QUESTION STAYS OPEN. `TAVILY_API_KEY` is not configured, so `research_search` refuses (no-credential, DEC-0006). The credential-free `research_fetch` path does work, so three claims were taken from primary Next.js documentation (v16.3.2, retrieved 2026-08-24) and recorded as assertions with quote-verified evidence: AST-0015 (dev and production are DIFFERENT builds — `.next/dev` versus `.next`), AST-0016 (`next start` is production mode and requires a prior `next build`), and AST-0017 (a self-hosted Node.js deployment supports all Next.js features, with no platform or adapter required). ⚠️ AST-0015 IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS FOR THE TRIGGER: because the two builds are genuinely different artifacts, a validation run under `next dev` says nothing about what a production deployment does — which is precisely why #137 could defer AST-0010 while the mode was undeclared, and why declaring production mode makes it owed rather than optional. ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, and why the question is not being closed: these three establish the MECHANICS, not the CHOICE. All three sit at rung 2 (`source-supported`) — documentation, not measurement — and the open half is operational rather than documentary: whether a long-lived `next dev` process is sound as the shipped configuration for a local tool, and whether its own file watching interacts badly with the app's chokidar watcher (#73), which bears on REQ-0018 and QST-0021 as much as on this question. Neither is answerable from a documentation page: the first needs discovery across reports the docs do not carry, and the second needs a bounded probe. Closing this now would be deciding a product question from mechanics alone and calling the result researched. ⚠️ HOST PROBE RUN 2026-08-25 — AND IT DOES NOT CLOSE THIS QUESTION. AST-0018 (rung 3, experimentally-validated, EVD-0021) establishes that a concurrent `next dev` did not measurably interfere with a chokidar watcher on the same tree: 20/20 files observed in all three runs, at latency indistinguishable from controls taken before AND after the treatment, with no recompile triggered by the content writes. That removes ONE argument against `next dev` — the one this project had specific reason to fear, given #73. ⚠️ It removes an argument; it does not make the decision. The probe ran for under a minute, so the real concern behind this question — whether a long-lived `next dev` is sound as the SHIPPED configuration over hours — is untouched, and is recorded as an omission on EVD-0021 rather than quietly left out. The scenario also put the watched directory inside the Next.js project root; the application may watch a content root outside it entirely. And the deployment-mode choice still turns on the trade AST-0015 describes: `next dev` ships an artifact that is not the production one, so choosing it means shipping a configuration this project can never validate as production — while choosing production reopens AST-0010 immediately (#137). That is a product judgement about which cost to accept, and no probe decides it. ⚠️ Still owed before this can close: discovery on long-lived dev-server behaviour, which needs search results direct retrieval cannot supply (TAVILY_API_KEY unset).
statement: The application shell must declare ONE deployment mode as its supported configuration. Choosing production mode reactivates AST-0010, which was deferred (#137) on the grounds that validating a production build would test an undeclared deployment mode.

answer: Stage documents are restricted MDX, compiled AT REQUEST TIME with `@mdx-js/mdx` — not routed as `@next/mdx` file-based pages, which compile the document into the build and cannot satisfy REQ-0018. A remark plugin rejects, with file and line:column, every import/export, expression, JSX attribute expression, spread attribute, and unmapped component; forbidden JavaScript is an error, never a silent removal, and stripping stays underneath as defence in depth only. The permitted set is the component mapping, which becomes the complete set of reachable components once imports are refused. The question's original premise was wrong: MDX has no allowlist to configure, so the allowlist is produced by subtraction at compile time. Validated in both compilation modes. The compiler and plugin chain are pinned; changing either reopens security validation. See DEC-0020.
notes: ⚠️ The load-bearing property is that agent-authored content must NOT implicitly become arbitrary application code. This project's whole discipline is that content is data the tool reads (#88 forbids authoring artifacts by hand precisely so the writer is a typed operation) — a document format whose default is 'anything in scope is callable' inverts that. The answer needs three parts: where compilation happens, the allowlist of components a document may use, and the behaviour on an unknown reference (refuse, or render inert). Refusing is consistent with how `checkJob` treats a shell-string command: refused rather than sanitised, because sanitising means guessing what the author meant. ⚠️ PRIMARY-DOCUMENT PASS 2026-08-26 (AST-0023, AST-0024, AST-0025; EVD-0025..EVD-0033, every claim quote-verified). STILL UNANSWERED, and deliberately so — search-backed discovery of failure reports and operational constraints has not been possible, and those could change the component-boundary decision. ⚠️ WHAT THE DOCUMENTATION SETTLES. Part 1 — compilation happens in the bundler through `@next/mdx`, and a root `mdx-components` file is mandatory. Part 2 — THE PREMISE IS WRONG: there is no allowlist to configure. MDX documents may import ESM and contain whole JavaScript programs, and the component mapping substitutes rather than restricts. Part 3 — an unresolved reference throws at runtime, which is a diagnostic for a mistaken author and not a boundary against a capable one. ⚠️ WHAT IS LEFT IS A PRODUCT JUDGEMENT, NOT A RESEARCH GAP. MDX's own position is that safety rests on trusting the author. So the question becomes whether agent-authored stage documents are trusted code — and #88 forbids hand-authoring artifacts precisely because the writer should be a typed operation. Reading more documentation will not settle that. ⚠️ WHAT SEARCH IS STILL OWED, and why it is worth waiting for: whether anyone has run agent-authored or otherwise semi-trusted MDX in production and what went wrong; whether restricting the compiler (rejecting ESM and expression nodes via a plugin) is something projects actually do or something that breaks in practice; and the operational cost of the alternative — compiling stage documents as plain markdown and rendering MDX only for a fixed set of authored pages. Those are failure reports, not specifications, and direct retrieval cannot find them. ⚠️ IT ALSO CONSTRAINS AND IS CONSTRAINED BY REQ-0021. If a document may reference components, the permitted set is another surface a direct planning-content read could enter through, so static confinement has to cover it. ⚠️ AND NOTHING HERE SETTLES CACHE COMPONENTS: DEC-0019 was chosen so the read contract holds with that flag either way, and no finding above touches it. ⚠️ SEARCH-BACKED PASS 2026-08-26 (AST-0026, AST-0027, AST-0028; EVD-0034..EVD-0040 plus EVD-0041). The credential arrived and the three things this question was held open for are now answered. (1) Has anyone run semi-trusted MDX and what went wrong — YES: CVE-2026-0969, CWE-94, high severity, arbitrary code execution during SSR of untrusted MDX. (2) Is restricting the compiler real practice or does it break — REAL, and now the DEFAULT: `next-mdx-remote` 6.0.0 blocks JS expressions unless asked otherwise, and ESM removal is an off-the-shelf remark plugin. (3) The cost of the alternative — reframed by the finding below, because the choice is not MDX versus markdown but WHICH MDX. ⚠️ PROPOSAL, NOT A DECISION (#34, stage 5 is agent-proposes-user-approves). Compile stage documents with expression nodes and `mdxjsEsm` nodes REMOVED, so a document is markdown plus the component vocabulary the mapping supplies and nothing else. That is the allowlist the question originally asked for, produced by subtraction at compile time rather than by a permitted set — which is what the ecosystem converged on after the CVE, and it is the only form that makes AST-0024's runtime error the ONLY way an unknown reference can fail. ⚠️ THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDES IT IS LOCAL, NOT ECOSYSTEM-WIDE. The handoff package ships stage documents verbatim to other people. Unrestricted MDX would hand recipients executable agent-authored documents; and because the publisher filters on `.md`, the lazy version of the change makes all nine documents silently vanish from the package instead. A restricted compile avoids both. ⚠️ NOT YET MEASURED, and this is what is owed before the proposal can be accepted: that the subtraction composes with `@next/mdx`'s build-time integration at all, that a document using a mapped component still renders once expressions are gone, and that the publisher's filter is updated deliberately rather than by omission. Every claim above is source-supported; nothing has been compiled. ⚠️ STILL DOES NOT SETTLE CACHE COMPONENTS, and REQ-0021 still applies to whatever is chosen: if a document may reference components, static confinement of planning-content reads has to cover that surface too.
statement: Stage documents under `planning-content/stages/` are agent-authored content. MDX compiles to executable JavaScript, so the compilation strategy must state which components a document may reference and what happens to a reference outside that set.
title: How is MDX compiled, and which components may a stage document execute?

answer: Two views. `/` is the project view — derived current stage, navigation across all nine stages with gate state, truthful artifact counts, lint findings surfaced. `/stage/[stageId]` is the stage view — the working document as restricted MDX, exit criteria with attestations, and typed review actions. Both URL-addressable and server-rendered, with no correctness-critical state held only in the client: transient interface state is fine, but anything a user must not lose is URL-encoded or persisted, because DEC-0022 reloads the page on every change and every reconnection. The artifact tracker and the assertion/evidence view are deferred to roadmap step 5, not removed. See DEC-0023.
notes: The vertical slice as scoped needs a stage view at minimum, because it displays the current stage and one stage document. `app/server.mjs` already renders an assertion/evidence view against the same substrate, so that view has a working reference implementation and is the cheapest to reach parity on — which is an argument about ORDER, not about what the first slice must contain. ⚠️ ANSWERED LAST, AND NOT BY RESEARCH (pm, 2026-08-24). This is principally a PRODUCT decision, not a research question: no source settles which views a planning tool should open with. It is sequenced fifth so it is decided under the constraints the other four establish rather than ahead of them — a deployment mode (QST-0017), a component bound on what a document may execute (QST-0018), a server/client module boundary (QST-0020) and a runtime lifecycle (QST-0021) each remove options from the information architecture before it is chosen. Choosing the IA first would mean designing views against constraints nobody had established, and then rediscovering them. ⚠️ PROPOSED 2026-08-27, AFTER THE OTHER FOUR CLOSED, and no search credit was spent because this question said not to: no source settles which views a planning tool opens with. What the sequencing bought is not evidence but ELIMINATION — four decisions now remove options that would otherwise have been discovered by building them. ⚠️ WHAT THE CONSTRAINTS ACTUALLY REMOVE (the first two are logical consequences of the decisions, not measurements, and are flagged as such). (a) DEC-0022 makes every content change and every reconnection a FULL PAGE RELOAD. So no view may hold state the reload would destroy: open panels, active tabs, scroll-restored lists and client-side filters are out of the first slice unless they are encoded in the URL. This is the sharpest constraint and it is the one that would have been discovered last. (b) DEC-0019 blocks prefetching as an accepted cost, so every navigation is a round trip with no warm-up. That argues for FEWER, DENSER views rather than many thin ones a user would page through — an inference from the accepted cost, not something measured. (c) DEC-0020 compiles stage documents per request, at a cost that is explicitly unmeasured. A view that rendered several documents at once would multiply an unknown, so: at most ONE stage document per view until that cost is measured. (d) DEC-0021 exposes only what the shell needs through `app/server/*`, and holds back locking and process-spawning modules for individual review. Read-only views are cheap; the review-status write goes through the locking path and is the one capability the first slice must actually get reviewed and exposed. (e) DEC-0022's truthful-count rule binds every summary surface: a tracker or dashboard that reports totals must report only what it rendered. ⚠️ PROPOSAL — TWO VIEWS, both URL-addressable, both server-rendered, no client state. `/` — the project view: the derived current stage (REQ-0016), all nine stages with their gate state, artifact counts under the truthful-count rule, and lint findings surfaced rather than re-judged (#47). `/stage/[stageId]` — the stage view: that stage's document as restricted MDX (REQ-0017), its exit criteria with recorded attestations, and the review-status action through the typed write path (REQ-0019). That is the whole first slice. It satisfies REQ-0016 through REQ-0019 and nothing else, and both views survive an arbitrary reload because neither holds state. ⚠️ DEFERRED, WITH REASONS RATHER THAN SILENCE. The artifact tracker and the assertion/evidence view are deferred even though the SKELETON ALREADY IMPLEMENTS THE LATTER — DEC-0017 keeps `app/server.mjs` as the verified substrate reference until the new shell reaches parity, so that view has a working home today and reaching parity on it is roadmap step 5, not step 4. Authoring, search, graph and cross-stage navigation are out: none is required by REQ-0016..0019, and each would add state the reload contract forbids or a surface the count rule would then have to cover. ⚠️ WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS. If per-request MDX compilation is measured to be expensive (DEC-0020's third obligation), the stage view is where it hurts, and the fallback is that decision's own second alternative — plain markdown — rather than a different information architecture. And if reload-on-change proves too coarse in use, the answer is a finer change signal, not client-held state; the reload contract is what makes the missed-change class of defect impossible. ⚠️ STILL A PM DECISION (#34). Recorded as a proposal; the question stays unanswered until it is approved. ⚠️ AND IT DOES NOT SETTLE CACHE COMPONENTS: nothing above depends on that flag, which is the property DEC-0019 was chosen to preserve.
statement: The first slice must choose which views exist: project overview, stage view, artifact tracker, assertion/evidence view, or some subset. The choice determines what the vertical slice has to render and what it may defer.
title: What is the initial information architecture of the application shell?

answer: The shell imports `lib/` by plain relative path — no alias, no `transpilePackages`, nothing special — but only through a thin `app/server/*` adapter layer. Each adapter imports `server-only` first, re-exports by explicit name or wrapper rather than `export *`, and exposes only what the shell needs; process-spawning, locking and stateful modules are reviewed individually. No app code outside `app/server/` imports `lib/` directly, and REQ-0021's static check enforces that and detects bypasses. `lib/` stays unmarked so the CLIs and the test suite keep working under plain Node. The guard does not prevent anything the build did not already prevent; it makes the failure locatable. See DEC-0021.
notes: ⚠️ The constraint is #47's own: one implementation, several callers. The app is the second caller the lint was designed for. The real difficulty is that these modules are Node-only — they read the filesystem, take locks and spawn processes — so the boundary between what runs on the server and what reaches the client is the actual subject of this question, not the import syntax. ⚠️ MEASURED 2026-08-26 (AST-0032, AST-0033; EVD-0045..EVD-0048 sourced, EVD-0049 and EVD-0050 experimental). PROPOSAL MADE, NOT DECIDED — stage 5 is agent-proposes-user-approves (#34). ⚠️ THE IMPORT MECHANISM IS A NON-PROBLEM, which is worth saying plainly because the question assumed otherwise: a Server Component imports a sibling `lib/` module by plain relative path and it builds and runs. No alias, no `transpilePackages`, no bundler configuration. #47's single implementation needs nothing special to stay single. ⚠️ THE REAL SUBJECT IS THE BOUNDARY, as the question's own note predicted, and the documented hazard is transitive: a `'use client'` file drags ALL of its imports into the client bundle (EVD-0046). Both client-import cases already fail the build — so the risk is not that Node-only code ships to a browser, it is that the failure is UNREADABLE. Unguarded, Turbopack reports an internal error with `location: undefined` and no filename. ⚠️ PROPOSAL: a thin `app/server/*` adapter layer carrying `import 'server-only'` and re-exporting from `lib/`, with application code importing the adapter and never `lib/` directly. Measured to work in both directions, and it is forced rather than chosen — the guard CANNOT go in `lib/`, because `server-only` throws under plain Node and `lib/` is imported by every `bin/` command and the whole test suite. ⚠️ IT WANTS REQ-0021'S CHECK, NOT A SECOND ONE. The adapter is a convention until something enforces it; a component can import `../../lib/x.mjs` and bypass the guard. That is the same static-confinement rule REQ-0021 already requires for planning-content reads, with a second forbidden edge rather than a new mechanism. ⚠️ NOT MEASURED: whether every module the shell needs can be re-exported this way — some take locks, spawn processes, or hold module-level state — and whether the unguarded failure differs under webpack. ⚠️ NOTHING HERE TOUCHES CACHE COMPONENTS.
statement: The shell must consume the existing lint, derivation, locking and typed-operation modules as the single implementation (#47), rather than reimplementing any of them inside the application. The mechanism — path resolution, bundling behaviour, and which modules may run in a browser context at all — is unsettled.
title: How does the Next.js shell import lib/ without duplicating it?

answer: A documented launcher owns the `next start` process. The watcher lives INSIDE that process: the change-stream service creates it on the first subscription and closes it when the last subscriber leaves, and terminating the process releases any that remains through process teardown. The launcher terminates its child and leaves nothing behind, verified by observation. Stream health is a NAMED heartbeat event plus a client watchdog that renders a visibly disconnected state — comment keepalives are ignored by the client parser and cannot serve. A watcher failure emits a visible signal or closes the stream; logging alone is not permitted. On reconnection the client reloads, treating reconnection as a change hint, so no event buffer or `Last-Event-ID` is needed. Malformed content is surfaced and located, and no rendered count may include an artifact the page did not render. See DEC-0022.
notes: ⚠️ Each of these already has a partial answer in the skeleton and none of them is written down as a contract. #73 records that `fs.watch` is unusable on Windows and chokidar is not, so the watcher choice is settled; its LIFETIME is not. The SSE reconnect behaviour matters more than it looks: a dropped stream that silently never reconnects leaves the operator reading stale state while the page looks live, which is the same class of defect as a retained workspace reported as destroyed. ⚠️ MEASURED 2026-08-27 (AST-0034, AST-0035; EVD-0055, EVD-0056, plus EVD-0051..EVD-0054 from the WHATWG specification). PROPOSAL MADE, NOT DECIDED — stage 5 is agent-proposes-user-approves. ⚠️ THE QUESTION'S OWN PREDICTION WAS RIGHT, AND UNDERSTATED. It said a silently dead stream is the same class of defect as a retained workspace reported destroyed. Measurement says the skeleton has that defect twice over and by construction: an idle stream emits ZERO bytes, so idle and dead are byte-identical, and no `id:` is ever sent, so a change during a reconnect gap is lost with nothing to recover it from. ⚠️ PROPOSAL, five parts. (1) INSTALLATION — the shell installs with the package and runs from one documented command; the detail belongs to REQ-0020 and is not settled here. (2) STARTUP — `next build` then `next start` per DEC-0018, with the watcher created as the server begins listening. (3) WATCHER LIFETIME — bound to the server process: created on listen, closed in the server's own `close()`, which the skeleton already does. ⚠️ Add what it does NOT do: there is no `watcher.on('error')` handler, so a watcher that dies takes the refresh guarantee with it and says nothing — the same defect as the stream, one layer down. (4) SSE RECONNECT — three changes, and the third is the one that removes a whole class of work. (a) A periodic comment frame, so idle and dead stop being byte-identical. (b) A client `onerror` that renders a visible disconnected state rather than leaving a live-looking page. (c) TREAT RECONNECTION ITSELF AS A CHANGE HINT and reload on it — because events are hints and never deltas (#73), a reconnecting client that reloads is exactly caught up, so `Last-Event-ID` and server-side event buffering are not needed at all. (5) ERROR HANDLING — a malformed or unreadable artifact must be visible and located, and the header must never report a count it did not render. Reporting `178` while showing 177 is worse than showing an error, because it tells the operator the missing thing is present. ⚠️ NOT MEASURED: browser reconnect behaviour (no `EventSource` in this Node build and no browser on this host — the client half is specification-only), idle timeouts beyond six seconds, concurrent clients, and malformation modes other than invalid JSON. ⚠️ NOTHING HERE TOUCHES CACHE COMPONENTS. ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-29: THERE IS NO SECOND PROCESS, AND THERE NEVER WAS ONE TO OWN. This artifact previously said the launcher owns 'both the application process and the file watcher' and 'terminates the watcher with the application'. The watcher is chokidar, imported dynamically INSIDE the `next start` process and held by the change-stream service in that process's memory. A parent launcher cannot call `changeStream.close()` across that boundary without adding IPC or a shutdown endpoint, and neither is justified for a local-first tool. The old wording described a mechanism that could not be built, which is worse than an unmet obligation: it would have been 'satisfied' by a launcher that called nothing and reported success. ⚠️ WHAT IS TRUE INSTEAD, and all of it is enforceable. The launcher owns ONE child: the `next start` process. The change-stream service owns its watcher and closes it when its last subscriber leaves — already built and tested under TSK-0011. Terminating the application process releases any watcher still open through process teardown, which is the operating system's guarantee rather than the launcher's. `close()` stays what it is: a service and test lifecycle operation, never something the launcher claims to call across a process boundary. ⚠️ THE PROPOSAL'S CLAUSE (3), 'WATCHER LIFETIME — created on listen, closed in the server's own close(), which the skeleton already does', IS WHERE THIS ENTERED. It was a true statement about the SKELETON, which owned its own HTTP server, and it was carried forward into a design with no such object. The note beside it even said the pattern might not carry to `next start` — the caveat was recorded and then the conclusion was used anyway.
statement: The application is installed and run locally by the operator. Its lifecycle must be specified: how it is installed, how it starts, how long the file watcher lives relative to the server process, what a client does when the SSE stream drops, and what the operator sees when content is malformed or unreadable.
title: What are the shell's installation, startup, watcher-lifetime, SSE-reconnect and error-handling behaviours?

notes: ⚠️ FOUND BY NEEDING IT, not by auditing — the fourth time this project has hit that pattern (#83's missing lifecycle setter, #126's missing question resolver, #132's missing migration, QST-0010's missing activation operation). The watcher-interaction probe for QST-0021 could not be expressed: `commands` is an array of argument arrays run one after another with `shell: false`, so 'start a server, measure something else, stop the server' has no representation. A literal '&' would be passed as an argument, which is the argument-array design working correctly. ⚠️ TWO separate blockers, and only one is an authorisation question. The ceiling refused the job first, on `requires: { network: true }` — that is #77 working, and the PM can raise it. The missing service form is not an authorisation question at all and no ceiling change reaches it. ⚠️ The alternative is not obviously worse: a host probe recorded honestly as `execution: "host"` with its omissions is what #131's reshape made recordable, and it is what actually answered the question. A `services: []` form would add real containment and disposal to this class of validation — but it is controller work, and it should earn its own commitment rather than being built inside an application question (#106). ⚠️ TRIGGER for building it: the first claim where host execution is not good enough — anything needing containment, a clean environment, or a result someone outside this machine must trust.
statement: The validation controller runs declared commands sequentially to completion and has no form for a service that must stay running while something else is observed. Any claim about two processes interacting is therefore unvalidatable under the controller, whatever the approved ceiling permits.
title: Should the tier-1 job model support long-lived services, or are host probes the answer for concurrent-process validation?

answer: Every server-side planning-content read awaits `connection()` before the filesystem read, inside a `<Suspense>` boundary whose fallback is a real loading state for that content. Chosen over `io()` and `export const dynamic` because it is the only measured mechanism that is fresh with Cache Components both enabled and disabled, so the freshness contract does not depend on a caching decision nobody has taken. Its cost — `connection()` blocks prefetching — is accepted, not deferred. See DEC-0019; measured in EVD-0023.
notes: ⚠️ CREATED BY EVIDENCE, not by planning: this question did not exist until the AST-0010 validation produced AST-0019. It blocks REQ-0016 (current stage display), REQ-0017 (MDX stage document) and REQ-0018 (external-change refresh) — all three read content that the agent and the PM write externally, and all three would silently serve build-time state under the configuration DEC-0018 just adopted. ⚠️ It is a STAGE 5 question, not a research one. The mechanisms are documented; which one this application uses is a design choice, and it belongs with the components at roadmap step 3a. ⚠️ Note what it does NOT reopen: DEC-0018 stands. Production mode was chosen because the shipped artifact must be the validated one, and this finding argues for that decision rather than against it — the freeze is exactly the class of behaviour that never appears under `next dev`. ⚠️ CANDIDATES MEASURED 2026-08-25 (EVD-0023, AST-0020) — DESIGN PROPOSED, NOT YET DECIDED. Stage 5 is agent-proposes-user-approves (#34), so this question stays open until the PM approves a contract. The measured matrix rules out more than it rules in: the baseline freezes in both models; `export const dynamic` does not exist under Cache Components; `connection()` alone fails the BUILD under Cache Components; and `io()` behind Suspense is fresh only with Cache Components on, going silently stale if it is ever turned off. ⚠️ The proposal is `connection()` behind a Suspense boundary for every route that reads planning content, because it is the only measured option that does not require the caching model to be decided first — which keeps this question inside the freshness contract instead of quietly settling Cache Components on its behalf. Its cost is that it blocks prefetching, and that belongs in the decision rather than in a footnote.
statement: Under `next build` + `next start`, a Server Component that reads an artifact synchronously is prerendered as a static route and serves its build-time value indefinitely. The application shell must therefore choose an explicit mechanism — a dynamic route, a read through a dynamic API, a revalidation strategy, or client-side fetching — for every view that must reflect external content changes.
title: How does the application make artifact-reading routes reflect external writes in production mode?

notes: ⚠️ FOUND BY DOING IT, 2026-08-27. The command was run to check whether closing stage 5 had cleared the last blocker. It had — and the run published 22 files and moved the package snapshot from 6c86330767dcbbfa to 3c7d695551d607ce. The change was reverted with `git checkout` before anything was committed, but the point is that a status check cannot be performed without the side effect. ⚠️ THE COST IS NOT THE ACCIDENT, IT IS THE INCENTIVE. Publication is supposed to be a deliberate act — DEC-0009 chose an explicit deterministic command precisely so the gate stays read-only and publishing is never a side effect of evaluation. That decision is honoured in one direction only: the gate does not publish, but the only exposed way to READ the gate does. ⚠️ THE DESIGN IS OPEN, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A QUESTION AND NOT A REQUIREMENT. Plausible shapes: a `--check` flag on the existing command, a separate `handoff:check` script, or exposing `handoffCompleteness` through a small status command that the app could also use. All three are cheap; none is obviously right, and the third overlaps with what CMP-0015 needs anyway. ⚠️ RECORDED AS A QUESTION RATHER THAN A REQUIREMENT ON PURPOSE. Stage 5's `requirements-traced-to-components` is attestation-only, so authoring a requirement here would NOT trip the gate — it would simply make the attestation written today silently false, which is worse than a visible regression. A question tracks the gap without claiming a design or quietly invalidating a judgement someone just made. ⚠️ NOT TO BE BUILT AS A DETOUR. The application shell is the work in progress; this is a one-command convenience in the tool that surrounds it. It belongs in a later cycle unless someone publishes by accident and does not notice, which is the trigger that would make it urgent.
statement: `npm run handoff` is the only way to learn whether the gates pass, and it PUBLISHES: on success it replaces `docs/plan/` with a new package. There is no read-only form, so checking readiness and performing publication are the same act, and anyone who wants the first necessarily performs the second.
title: How is handoff readiness inspected without publishing?

notes: ⚠️ NON-BLOCKING FOR v1, BY DECISION. The observed 245-375 ms stage response is accepted for a local-first tool on a developer's own machine while the attribution stays open. This is recorded so the unknown stays visible, not so it blocks. ⚠️ IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE FIRST ANSWER WAS WRONG AND CONFIDENT. The span was initially reported as a per-request read of all 253 artifacts. It is not — `lintProject` is not on `readStageDocument`'s path at all. The plausible story was accepted without being measured, which is the same mistake DEC-0020's fallback made about the compiler. Twice now on one measurement, an assumed cause has been wrong; the instruction to instrument before optimising is that pattern being taken seriously. ⚠️ THE CONTENTION HYPOTHESIS IS THE INTERESTING ONE, because if it holds, the cost is not in this read at all — it is the whole-project lint running beside it, and it would move if either boundary changed. It is also the one most easily missed by instrumenting only inside `readStageDocument`. ⚠️ A SEVENTH RUN MEASURED THE READ AT 104.88 ms MEDIAN / 117.12 ms p95 — a THIRD of the 234-359 ms this question was opened about, from the same code against the same content on the same host. The span is not a stable cost, and that is itself the strongest evidence so far: work that is genuinely I/O-bound on nine small files does not vary threefold. It moves the contention hypothesis ahead of the other two, because the thing most likely to differ between runs is what the sibling `<Suspense>` boundary was doing at the time — `readStageCriteria` lints and validates every artifact in the project concurrently with this read. ⚠️ IT ALSO MEANS ACC-0020 WAS DECIDED BY NOISE. Six runs split 3/3 across a 300 ms line while the underlying cost ranged at least 117-359 ms; a seventh run would have passed it. That is the sharpest argument for why the criterion was replaced rather than re-run until it passed. ⚠️ STILL DO NOT OPTIMISE ON THIS. Threefold variance is consistent with contention, with filesystem cache state, and with the `connection()` wait behaving differently under load — the same three candidates, none eliminated. Instrument the three separately first.
statement: `readStageDocument` measured 234-359 ms p95 across six runs. It awaits `connection()`, lists the stage directory and reads nine files totalling roughly 90 KB — work that should cost single-digit milliseconds. Which part of that span is actually spending the time, and is it reducible? INSTRUMENT BEFORE OPTIMISING: the three candidates are the `connection()` wait itself, the directory listing plus nine reads, and contention with the sibling `<Suspense>` boundary on the same request — `readStageCriteria` calls `lintProject`, which reads and validates every artifact in the project, concurrently with this read. Nothing has separated them, so all three remain live and none may be assumed.
title: What accounts for the 234-359 ms stage-document read?
